prompt: You triple your speed from 20 mph to 60 mph. About how much greater is the force of impact if you crash?
choices: About 3 times greater
About 6 times greater
About 9 times greater
About 12 times greater
explanation: Impact force grows with the square of speed. Doubling your speed makes the force of impact (and the braking distance) about 4 times greater; tripling it makes them about 9 times greater.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. FL pp.68, 76; KS p.59; LA p.70; AK p.33)

prompt: You see a red light well ahead and plan a normal, smooth stop. Which way of stopping is best?
choices: Keep your speed up, then brake hard close to the stop line
Shift into neutral early and coast the rest of the way to the line
Turn on your hazard flashers and brake at the last moment
Check mirrors, ease off the gas, then brake with steady pressure
explanation: For a smooth stop, check your mirrors for traffic behind you, release the accelerator early so the car slows, then press the brake with steady pressure, which also lights your brake lights. Sudden, late stops invite rear-end crashes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. FL p.76, CO p.9, KS p.30, KY p.41)

prompt: How do the rights and duties of motorcycle riders on public roads compare with those of car drivers?
choices: Riders have fewer rights and must yield to cars
They are the same, and riders must obey the same traffic laws
Riders have extra rights, so cars must always yield to them
They are the same, but riders can't be ticketed for most violations
explanation: Motorcyclists have the same rights and responsibilities on the road as other drivers. A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane, and riders who break traffic laws can be ticketed like anyone else.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. FL p.93, CA p.50, CT p.20, IL p.44, MD p.39)

prompt: Mile for mile, why is driving on city streets usually riskier than driving on an expressway?
choices: They have cross traffic, intersections and pedestrians
Cars usually travel faster on city streets than on expressways
City streets carry more large trucks than expressways do
Expressways are lit at night, but city streets are not
explanation: Expressways have no intersections, traffic signals or cross traffic, pedestrians are kept off them, and traffic on each side moves the same way. City streets add all of these conflicts, so scan for cross traffic and people at every intersection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. MI p.74, NV p.36, MD p.31)

prompt: A sign at the curb reads 2 HOUR PARKING 8:30 AM – 5:30 PM. What does it mean?
choices: No parking at all from 8:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.
Parking is allowed only for 2 hours after 5:30 p.m.
From 8:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., you may park there for up to 2 hours
Only vehicles displaying a permit may park there during those hours
explanation: This sign allows parking but limits how long you may stay during the hours shown: here, up to 2 hours at a time between 8:30 a.m. and 5:30 p.m. Staying longer than the limit can get you a ticket.
ref: MUTCD Sec. 2B (parking signs); Michigan What Every Driver Must Know (Oct. 2025), p. 58

prompt: What does this sign warn you about?
choices: A bike lane starts ahead, and cars must stay out of it
Bicycles are not allowed to use the road beyond this point
A bicycle shop or rental is nearby
Bicyclists may be riding on or crossing the road ahead
explanation: This yellow diamond warning sign means bicyclists may be riding on the road or crossing it ahead. Slow down, watch for them and give them room. A sign that bans bicycles is a white regulatory sign with a red circle and slash.
ref: MUTCD Sec. 2C (W11-1); state driver handbooks (e.g. MI p.59, FL p.58, KS p.36, MD p.22)

prompt: What does this sign tell you?
choices: U-turns are allowed at the next intersection ahead
A roundabout is ahead; slow down and get ready to yield
Traffic from both sides will merge into your lane ahead
A recycling center or turnaround area is ahead
explanation: This yellow warning sign shows a circular intersection (roundabout) ahead. Slow down, watch for pedestrians at the crosswalks, and be ready to yield to traffic already in the roundabout.
ref: MUTCD Sec. 2C (W2-6); state driver handbooks (e.g. MI p.59, OR p.20, LA p.30, MO p.50)
